utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If they're public, they can be admitted in a public section as well. So we are now in open session again. Madam Registrar, could you please give the title and the numbers of the two intercepts.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number P282: Transcript of intercepted conversation between Momcilo Krajisnik and Mirko Krajisnik, dated 15 June 1992. And P282.1, the English translation. P283: Transcript of intercepted conversation between Momcilo Krajisnik and Mirko Krajisnik, dated 22 June 1992. P283.1, English translation. P284, map of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since there are no objections, they're admitted into evidence, not under seal, whereas the previous numbers are admitted under seal. Mr. Stewart, I think we have only one document which is both in the original language and in translation, and the Chamber will wait to receive the other documents unless you say we'll deal with the transcript and the portions read, it's sufficiently clear, and we could do even without --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I think we can already say that, Your Honour. Those were very short passages, and it does appear that the interpretation we had is, not surprisingly, more than adequate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, although -- yes. Only the officially translated document there, there might be some questions especially in the last lines as to whether the translation is correct or not, in relation to the question I put to the Defence where it said --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, that one, Your Honour. Yes. Yes, because we didn't have -- I'm thinking of those passages that were in fact interpreted orally this morning, where we wouldn't propose to have a further translation done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No, I do understand that you're referring to those.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So they'll not be tendered as documentary evidence but just read into the transcript. And -- yes. And then, Madam Registrar, we have one document, and that is?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit D27, Momcilo Krajisnik in an interview to Dnevnik of August 1993, and D27.1, the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No objection, therefore admitted into evidence. Then I finally have one other question, but I urge the parties to be very cautious because it was dealt with in closed session. We have two documents in support of the reasons, I'll give in a minute, the reasons why protective measures were asked by Witness 623. I think marking for identification when we're in closed session would be a proper way of dealing with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we will wait until we are in closed session sooner or later -- no. We can perhaps go into private session for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since we are in open session now, Madam Registrar, a decision has been taken in closed session last Monday, and that was a decision on a motion for protective measures, and that decision should be public, so its in the transcript of the 20th of September, 2004. One of the legal officers gave me the pages, but I just lost them. It's the part starting with the phrase "This is a decision on the Prosecution's motion for protective measures for Witness 623. The motion was filed confidentially on the 24th of August, 2004." That's the beginning of the part that will be now to the public, and it ends with the line, "The Prosecution motion is granted." It's a couple of pages further. So that is now part of the public record of this these proceedings. Mr. Hannis, is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We are, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And who is going to lead that witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts will be dealing with this witness for the Prosecution, Your Honour, although this is a witness who is a 92 bis witness here for cross-examination, and if I I'd like to be --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Mr. Margetts will be dealing with this witness for the Prosecution, Your Honour, although this is a witness who is here as a 92 bis witness called for cross-exam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if I may, Your Honour, I request to be excused at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are no protective measures, and it is Mr. Begovic, if --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: General Asim Dzambasovic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I think I got the wrong one on the list. Yes, then. Madam Usher would you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have an objection I'd like to make to one very substantial paragraph in his statement. It may be more convenient if I make that objection the witness comes in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- please tell us what your objection is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I'm just wondering if Your Honour has the relevant document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I haven't got it in front of me at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's the statement of this witness stated or signed on the 16th of October, 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Which I think must be coming up as one of the very earliest items.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the long statement, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour is right. It's the very long one. And my objection is to the penultimate paragraph. So that begins on page 29. Your Honour, I won't read through the whole thing, but if I may simply refer specifically to the first few lines. Does Your Honour see a paragraph beginning "As to the 'Ram Plan'" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I haven't found it yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So sorry, Your Honour. It's page 29.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I've got it in front of me. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Stewart, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. "As to the 'Ram Plan' or the Brana Plan, the Muslim officers did not know about this plan until after the war." So the Muslim officers includes them. "I read about such plans in a book," which he mentions, and then he mentions other books. "I only saw the JNA plans titled S1, S2, S2A. They followed the structure of containment." And then he continues another couple of lines down: "This Brana or Ram Plan idea matches with a view for Greater Serbia. I have reached this conclusion after studying the war plans, reading books and reports of the war. I am among a group of 20 or 30 officers who have studied this issue and the war. We reached the conclusion that this plan was the basis for the first or initial deployment of the JNA in Croatia." And I can short-circuit this for the moment, as part of my initial submission and objection, because over the page and then about four or five lines from the end of this long paragraph he says: "As to the Drina River and the siege of Sarajevo, this would be the last step in the frame. I do not believe that there are any military experts who can dispute this plan. It was --" and so on. And, really, that last passage I referred to points to the problem. This paragraph is plainly in substance expert evidence. Now, when a military officer comes along to give evidence as a factual witness, of course his specific professional experience is in the nature of expertise. Of course it is. He is expert to that extent. But that's not technically expert evidence. It is coming along and describing how your particular job is done, how your particular profession is exercised, your particular technical knowledge, and that's factual evidence. This is not. This, what he's talking about here, and the very fact that he, in effect, challenges other military experts to dispute the plan indicates just that. He is not presented to us as an expert witness. We have not come or indeed taken the steps to consult and match him and prepare for his cross-examination armed with expert witness guidance and expert consultant guidance. And unless there are -- there may be -- there may be isolated factual points in here legitimately within the realm of a factual witness, which the Prosecution so far as they're relevant and probative, couldn't be prevented from adducing in the normal way. But -- and if they wish to do that, then I suggest that they indicate what those might be. But otherwise, we ask for the whole of that paragraph to be excised from the -- well, it's 92 bis evidence but excised from the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Stewart's observations are correct. This witness is called as a fact witness, not an expert witness. He has previously appeared as an expert witness in this Tribunal, but on this occasion that's not the case. The paragraph in question, we concur that that is a paragraph more suitable to an expert and we are happy to have it excised. The only difficulty is that the order of Your Honours of 12 May 2004 in respect of the admission of the 92 bis evidence in fact admits this statement, including that paragraph, into the evidence. So that would need to be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say if we would follow both the Defence, and at this moment in this respect the Prosecution who shares the view of this to be expert evidence, then we would then have to take a decision that this part is not -- would not be admitted. Of course it's never too late to do such a thing. Of course not the whole paragraph is expert. I mean, the first line is that "Officers did not know about the plans until after the war." That's of course factual. Let's keep in mind at this moment that this, according to both parties, is expert -- well, mainly expert evidence, although not all of it, and we'll give a decision on that whether this is excluded from the 92 bis admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we are start on the basis of this understanding and -- yes. Then, Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dzambasovic, before giving evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Text will be handed out to you now by Madam Usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dzambasovic. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll first explain to you the procedure. Mr. Dzambasovic, the Prosecution has submitted to this Chamber written statements of interviews you gave before. The Defence has asked to put questions in this respect to you, but we first start with a short summary of what is in your statement so that the public will know what we're talking about. Mr. Margetts. Let me just see. Is there any -- there's no reference to the last paragraph of this statement in the summary, is it? It's not reflected specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that paragraph is not referred to in the summary. Just one matter before we proceed with the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honours' ruling of 12 May 2004 admitted the 13 June 2000 statement, the 16 October 2002 statement and referred to the attachments to those statements, stating that the Prosecution can make application at the end of the witness's evidence to have those attachments that they wish to have admitted into evidence admitted. We've provided a list of exhibits which has ten documents listed in it. The last two documents are not technically attachments to the statements. Both of these documents are quite voluminous, and there is extensive reference in the statements to these documents. But within the bounds of Your Honour's order of 12 May 2004, they technically could not being characterised as attachments. So just at this stage I wanted to raise the issue with Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When has the Defence been informed about documents outside the scope of the attachments to be submitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the potential list of documents including these documents was provided to the Defence, I believe, at the end of last week. The final list of documents that being the ten that you see today, was provided to the Defence yesterday. And if you see the description of the documents that's in the list before you, it specifically refers to the last two documents as documents referred to in the statements and in the other -- and in respect of the other documents, it specifically refers to them as attachments to the statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that it needs some close reading to -- but -- Mr. Stewart, is there any response to this observation?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Not really. I haven't had time to read them anyway, Your Honour, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So a final decision, then. And would you please indicate Mr. -- well, of course you're not going to examine the witness, so therefore we'll first wait until Mr. Stewart has at least had a glance on it and perhaps read it wholly, or Ms. Loukas, and then further see whether he has any response to your observations then, and then look at it ourselves as well so as to see whether or not this is material that is admissible, yes are no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Just one further matter on that issue, and that is that there is extensive reference to these documents in the statement, so the Prosecution does not see the need to examine the witness any further in regard to these documents and wouldn't be seeking leave to do so. Our application would be based on the comments that are already contained in the evidence that has been admitted pursuant to 92 bis (A).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would then refrain from any direct knowledge of these non-attachments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would then not need them? Is that the correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No, sorry, Your Honour. All I was saying was this: that these documents were not attached, and in terms of the basis upon which we are seeking there are admission into evidence, that basis is sufficiently established in the statements that have been made by the witness so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's clear. That's the basis on which you seek admission. But let's first see, perhaps tomorrow, what the respond of the Defence is. Yes. Then we now go to the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: The 92 bis summary of the witness Asim Dzambasovic is as follows: General Asim Dzambasovic is a retired General from the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He retired in the year 2000 after 30 years in the military. His evidence concerns the period from September 1990 to April 1992, when he was the chief of staff and deputy commander of the 216th Mountain Brigade of the JNA. During this period, General Dzambasovic was based at the command headquarters of the brigade in the municipality of Han Pijesak in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The commander of the 216th Brigade and General Dzambasovic's superior was Dragomir Milosevic. Milosevic's superior and the commander of the 4th corps of the JNA was the Serb General Vojislav Djurdjevac. During 1991, there were two formal orders for mobilisation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the first on 30 June 1991, and the second on 17 September 1991. The first mobilisation failed. Almost exclusively, Serbs responded to the second mobilisation resulting in an ethnic imbalance being created in the JNA. In addition to the recruitment of Serb men to the units of the JNA, the SDS party recruited men into volunteer units. Serb volunteer units were located in Milici in Vlasenica municipality, in Borike and Gucevo in Rogatica municipality and in Sokolac. In early 1992, these Serb volunteer units were subordinated to the 216th Mountain Brigade. The three battalions that constituted the 216th Mountain Brigade were formed in Serb-dominated areas. The 1st Battalion was formed in the village of Gucevo in Rogatica, the 2nd Battalion in Sokolac, and the 3rd Battalion in Milici in Vlasenica. By April 1992, the 216th Mountain Brigade was effectively a Serbian brigade and the JNA had become a Serb army. General Dzambasovic was excluded from the planning process in the high level command of the brigade. He was bypassed by Serb officers, who consulted directly with Colonel Milosevic. In early 1992, some of his duties were transferred away from him to his Serb deputies, and at this stage he was chief of staff on paper only, and did he not have real authority. From late 1991, weapons and ammunition were distributed from the JNA store to Serbs. SDS leaders from the municipalities of Vlasenica, Rogatica, Sokolac, Olovo and Kladanj had regular meetings with Colonel Milosevic in Han Pijesak. General Dzambasovic saw Rajko Kusic from Rogatica, Milan Tupajic from Sokolac, Rajko Dukic from Vlasenica and Todorovic from Han Pijesak meeting with Milosevic. General Dzambasovic raised these issues with Colonel Milosevic and also with the corps commander, General Djurdjevac. He told them that command and control was not being followed, that arms were being distributed, arms were being stolen from JNA stores, there was inadequate discipline, and he raised the issue of improper meetings taking place with political leaders. No investigations nor any other action was taken by either Milosevic or Djurdjevac to address these concerns. In early March 1992, orders relating to combat readiness were issued by the commander of the 2nd Military District General Milutin Kukanjac to all units in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The orders were expressed as preparations for defence. However, the military did not have any information that an attack was imminent or even that any attacking forces existed. On 4 April, 1992, General Dzambasovic was shown a document stating that all Serbs in the area of responsibility of the 216th Mountain Brigade were to be mobilised on the orders of the SDS. At this point, he realised there was no longer anyplace for him in the JNA. He met with Colonel Milosevic, and Milosevic told him that he could no longer guarantee his safety. He immediately left and made his way to Sarajevo. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart. The Defence has asked the witness to appear to be cross-examined. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Dzambasovic, you have given a number of statements, and the one I'm referring to at the moment for the record is the 13th of June, 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the statement that I had wasn't actually paragraph numbered but I don't think it's going to create an enormous problem. Looking at the English version, on page 4 of 8. I don't believe at the moment it's essential for the witness to have the statement. I'll put the points.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Dzambasovic, you said that by early 1992, there having been a mobilisation of a lot of Serb volunteers, these battalions, and they were the battalions of your brigade, were almost exclusively Serb. When you say "almost exclusively," can you give an idea of the relatively proportions? How many non-Serbs, in percentage terms, were at that point contained within those battalions?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can speak about these questions. I don't know how much detail you're interested in, but because I'm an eyewitness of all these events, I can speak about these things in great detail or in not such detail. The ethnic structure of the brigade, which was valid and according to which the brigade was replenished according to the rules of the military mobilisation, under that structure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me stop you. Try, to the best of your ability, to focus and to concentrate on the specific question put to you. If we need any further details, you can be sure that Mr. Stewart will ask you about them. So the question now only was: What was the percentage remaining non-Serbs in this battalion? So if you know or if you say, "Well, I wouldn't know but it's anything between 10 or 20," or "I know exactly, it's 17.6," tell us that. I know that -- at least I have to assume that you know far more than you'll be asked here, but we are under some time restraints, and therefore we have to ask you what is most relevant for the parties. So please concentrate on that, yes? So the question was what percentage, if you know, of non-Serbs were at that moment still in those battalions or that battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's the three battalions. The 1st Battalion of the brigade which you said moved to Rogatica, the 2nd Battalion which had moved to Sokolac and the 3rd Battalion which moved to Milici. That was your summary of those battalions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those battalions, yes, there were three battalions. They were combat units, the percentage of Serbs in those battalions was over 90 per cent [as interpreted]. At the time when the second mobilisation was carried out, this was from the 17th of September, so up until the 17th of September that figure, that percentage, was approximately the same,as relating to the Serbs and according to the Bosnian Muslims. The total percentage in the brigade, since the brigade is a part of all those units, in percentages there were more Bosniaks in the brigade. It was 54 per cent. And the rest were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So in the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So in -- by early 1992, which was the point in time that you were talking about in your statement, as far as these three battalions were concerned, 1st, 2nd, and 3rd Battalion -- first of all, overall in those battalions can we be clear what you say was the percentage of non-Serbs? Can I do it that way round and ask you what you consider to be the percentage of non-Serbs, please.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of 1992, the percentage was perhaps 1 to 2 per cent of non-Serbs, primarily thanking -- because of the officers who were in those units who were not Serbs. I include myself amongst those officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And was that for all practical purposes, was that percentage even across those three battalions or was there any significant difference between one and another?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC
utterances.text: The differences were very slight, practically immaterial. So I think the situation was more or less the same. In all the three battalions, the ethnic structure was mono-ethnic in the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to rise to my feet at the time, but in the answer to the initial question, there was a percentage quoted, and that percentage I heard as 98 per cent but seems to have been recorded in the transcript as 90 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I heard, as a matter of fact, is that it was more than 90 per cent, but if the witness said -- let's verify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We say we distinctly heard -- memories play tricks but we thought we heard "over 90 per cent" as what the witness said earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, a full hundred per cent makes Serbs and non-Serbs, so the 1 or 2 per cent goes a bit in the direction of 98, so perhaps you could clarify that. We understood your testimony to be, and I'm not sure about the moment in time, but to be that over 90 per cent were Serbs in these three battalions, where others understood it to be more than 98 per cent. What in you first answer about percentages, what did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I said over 90 per cent, thinking that it is practically impossible to say 100 per cent. But mostly it was probably between -- I cannot give you an exact figure, but it's perhaps over 98 per cent, even.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the logic and the arithmetic of the witness and me were entirely consistent. In fact, the reason I asked him to turn it the other way round and give the non-Serb percentage was precisely because over 90 per cent wasn't specific enough for the purpose. So we've got there eventually. We've actually got to where we were to start with as it happens, but never mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness, thank you.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In the Han Pijesak, if I've got that right, barracks, you said there was a big warehouse that contained all the weapons and ammunition for the Territorial Defence units in the surrounding area. Then you said from the beginning of 1992 until April, that must have April 1992 when you left, the old system for accounting for the inflow and outflow of weapons and ammunition was totally ignored. Now, I just want to clarify with you. Are you saying that there was, in fact, no -- no proper control any more?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. In our barracks, there were warehouses which were guarded by the JNA about ten -- and they were the weapons of some ten municipalities from that area of Eastern Bosnia. The attitude towards the weapons and guarding them was very strict as far as the JNA was concerned when that was -- when they were there. Then, in that period, all the standards and norms vis-a-vis guarding the weapons ceased to be applied. The warehouses were broken into, equipment and weapons were stolen, and the authorised bodies did nothing to prevent that. That was the essence. Weapons were being trucked away without any kind of order. Up until that time, no one -- no one could even bring in a bullet, not even a man could enter the barracks without monitoring. But after that, trailer trucks without any proper papers would arrive at the barracks, without anything. Equipment was being driven away. Nobody knew where it was being taken, what was the reason for that. There were no documents. That was the problem. I informed my superior command about these events, but nobody did anything to prevent this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So, Mr. Dzambasovic, you've described elsewhere in your statements how, when the system had been operating properly as you indicated a moment ago, even a single round of ammunition had to be and was properly accounted for. That was the position, wasn't it? Now, the -- and you're nodding. The situation we got into, then, by early 1992, can you confirm it included these elements: First of all, you say it included the movement of weapons in and out of the weapons warehouse without them then being properly logged and accounted for and presumably without the proper paperwork being done; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC
utterances.text: Not only the paperwork, but there was real chaos. I can spend half a day giving you details about how when the vehicles came who accompanied the vehicles. I could give the names of those people. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond The authorities from the superior command who had the technical means and equipment to prove this, and you as lawyers know what all of that implies, none of them wanted to implement this. They pretended as if nothing had happened, which was absurd. It would be absurd in an earlier period. It is something that should not have been allowed to happen. If something like that were allowed to happen, I would have been replaced, the commander, the person in charge of guarding the warehouse. At the time, all of this was left aside and for us professional officers, the chaos that ensued was a very big surprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Witness, half a day's description will be beyond any legal, military, or any other duty, so I won't press you for that. But it is correct, then, in a nutshell the chaos which you say prevailed, did include movement of weapons in and out without any proper logging and accounting, and without any proper paperwork. It included that as an element; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. This was done illegally and secretly and in all possible illegal ways. Even fuel canisters were used to carry ammunition. I found on a couple of occasions a soldier putting bullet by bullet, filling bullet by bullet, fuel canisters so that you would not be able to tell that they were using them to carry ammunition. All of these things were done by members of the Serb ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And a second element you mentioned, break-ins. Was there a breakdown then of just basic security of the premises?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC
utterances.text: No. There was security personnel, but those "security" officers did not see or did not want to see that weapons were being stolen, taken away, removed from that location. I confirmed it in the following way: People were assigned to security who colluded in these activities. For example, a warehouse would be robbed in the course of the night. A tonne of equipment and materiel would be carried out and the soldiers there on guard duty would not see that. That is an absurd thing to say, that they would claim that they see anything. The security organs who were supposed to take measures, in whose jurisdiction it was, went on about their job as if nothing like that happened. So this was something that was just kept quiet about. But at meetings which I attended every day, things were said to the effect that we have to security the warehouses. We just find those responsible for removing and stealing the weapons. The perpetrators must be published. But none of that was actually implemented in practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The system that you describe, Mr. Dzambasovic, that -- would you agree, it clearly also opened up considerable scope for financial corruption as well, opportunities to sell weapons?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC
utterances.text: There were possibilities of all sorts to do that, financial possibilities and other types of possibilities for things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The warehouse of the Han Pijesak barracks was in a sort of valley surrounded by woods, so it was a very favourable location for those who were doing things like that. And these acts to take away the weapons were something that was done on the basis of agreement with the leadership in Han Pijesak and the surrounding settlements. I went to several places where I heard something like this. I happened to be in a restaurant on a couple of occasions, and I heard them talking about how they were going to take out weapons from the barracks, not being aware of the fact that I was an officer, a Bosniak, a Muslim. So they said that without being cautious. Actually, what I even said at meetings was -- and when people reported back to us, those who were responsible for that, these people would tell us what the problem was, but nothing was done to actually resolve these problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- see the clock. Well, I can't miss it from where I stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dzambasovic, we have to stop for the day. We'll resume tomorrow morning in Courtroom I, so not this same courtroom, at 9.00. I instruct you not to speak with anyone about your testimony once you've started. You should refrain from speaking to anyone, whether Prosecution, Defence, or any other person to speak about your testimony. I would first ask Madam Usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand, and thank you very much for that caution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, could you give us any impression of the time you need for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm really pretty confident that I would finish my --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you for reminding me. Your Honour, I'm pretty confident that I would be finished before the first break tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before the first break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because I noted that the witness has a lot to tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure that we're going to work together, Your Honour, with respect to make sure he tells us the essentials but not the utterly non-essential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd rather leave it primarily in your hands, but if you need any assistance, I'll certainly be glad to help.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. It's helpful to know where the task lies first in this structure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00, Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 23rd day of September, 2004, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.40 p.m.,
